\chapter{Friend and Siblings}
\label{ch:russian-friend-and-siblings}
\hlchaptermodality{7}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name a friend, brother and sister in Russian, build a feminine person-noun with \ru{по}-...-\ru{а}, and say which pronoun, \ru{ты} or \ru{вы}, goes with each.}

The chapter closes on \ru{сестра}, \ru{брат}'s securely cognate pair: the reader produces \ru{друг}, \ru{подруга}, \ru{брат} and \ru{сестра} with their genders, builds the \ru{по}-...-\ru{а} feminine pattern on \ru{подруга}, and names all four as exactly who Chapter 2's \ru{ты} was for. It reaches back to Chapter 5's \ru{брать}/\ru{брат} minimal pair and rescues three Chapter 2 atoms — the \ru{ты}/\ru{вы} comparison, the vy-politeness pragmatics, and the ty/thou etymology — that nothing had revisited since.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[drug]{\ru{друг} — \textquotedblleft{}friend,\textquotedblright{} the word that explains why \ru{ты} exists}

\label{lesson:RU-C07-drug}



\begin{quote}
A new chapter, and the first word in it names exactly who Chapter 2's informal \emph{\ru{ты}} was built for.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — \ru{друг}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ru{друг}} — \emph{drug} — \textbf{friend} (a man, or a friend generally)
\end{quote}

Consonant-final, so masculine — the ending rule holding steady for the third time. Every letter is one you already read — none of them the throat-rasp \textbf{\ru{х}} that \emph{\ru{хлеб}} just taught you; that one waits for a later word.

\emph{(Romanized, this word is spelled exactly like the English \textbf{drug} — pure accident of transliteration, no shared root at all. Say it }drook\emph{-ish, not like the English word it happens to resemble on the page.)}

This is the noun Chapter 2's whole \emph{\ru{ты}}/\emph{\ru{вы}} choice was about. \textbf{\ru{Ты}} is for a \emph{\ru{друг}} — someone close enough that formality would feel wrong. \textbf{\ru{Вы}} is for the stranger, the elder, the shopkeeper: everyone \emph{\ru{друг}} does not cover.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ru{друг}} is Indo-European *\emph{d\textsuperscript{h}rewg\textsuperscript{h}-}, \textquotedblleft{}to accompany, to be loyal\textquotedblright{} — a companion-on-the-road sense, not far from \emph{\ru{друг}}'s meaning today. Its clearest descendants sit outside everyday modern English: Gothic \textbf{gadrauhts}, \textquotedblleft{}warrior\textquotedblright{} (literally one who accompanies), and Old English \textbf{dryhten}, \textquotedblleft{}lord\textquotedblright{} — originally the leader a troop of \emph{drauhts} followed, a word that survives only in old poetry now, not in ordinary speech.

Unlike \emph{\ru{хлеб}}'s tidy modern cousin \emph{loaf}, this is a root that mostly vanished from English rather than one that thrived in it — worth saying plainly rather than stretching for a connection that isn't really there.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\ru{друг}\textquotedblright{} — masculine, consonant ending
  \item the pair — \textquotedblleft{}\ru{ты} for a \ru{друг}, \ru{вы} for everyone else\textquotedblright{}
  \item the false friend on paper — \textquotedblleft{}drug, spelled like the English word, unrelated to it\textquotedblright{}
  \item last chapter's letter — \textquotedblleft{}\ru{х}, the throat-rasp from \ru{хлеб}\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}friend.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{\ru{Друг}}.) Which pronoun goes with a \emph{\ru{друг}}, and which is for everyone else? (\textbf{\ru{Ты}} for a friend; \textbf{\ru{вы}} otherwise.) What did \emph{\ru{друг}}'s root originally mean? (\textbf{To accompany, to be loyal} — Gothic \emph{gadrauhts}, \textquotedblleft{}warrior\textquotedblright{}; English \emph{dryhten}, now archaic.) Is \emph{\ru{друг}} related to the English word it looks like on the page? (\textbf{No} — pure spelling coincidence.) And what English word is \emph{\ru{хлеб}}'s modern cousin? (\textbf{Loaf}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[podrúga]{\ru{подруга} — \textquotedblleft{}friend\textquotedblright{} (female), built on the word you just learned}

\label{lesson:RU-C07-podruga}



\begin{quote}
Russian doesn't reach for a new word to make \emph{\ru{друг}} feminine — it builds one, in front of your eyes, out of pieces you already have.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — \ru{подруга}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ru{подруга}} — \emph{podrúga} — \textbf{friend} (a woman)
\end{quote}

Ends in \textbf{-\ru{а}}, so feminine — the rule holding for the second time in this chapter, this time on a longer word.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: watch the word get built}]
Take \emph{\ru{друг}} apart and put it back together:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ru{по}-} (a prefix here worn down to little independent meaning) + \textbf{\ru{друг}} (friend) + \textbf{-\ru{а}} (the feminine ending) $\to$ \textbf{\ru{подруга}}
\end{quote}

This is Russian's ordinary machinery for turning a masculine person-word feminine: keep the root, change the ending, sometimes add a light prefix along the way. It is the same instinct English uses in \emph{host} $\to$ \emph{host-ess} or \emph{actor} $\to$ \emph{actr-ess} — a suffix doing the work — except Russian reaches for this pattern constantly, on ordinary words, not just a formal handful.

Say the pair together and the family resemblance is obvious:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ru{друг} · \ru{подруга}} — \emph{drug · podrúga}
\end{quote}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\ru{подруга}\textquotedblright{} — feminine, stress on the second syllable
  \item the build — \textquotedblleft{}\ru{по}- plus \ru{друг} plus -\ru{а}\textquotedblright{}
  \item the pair — \textquotedblleft{}\ru{друг}, \ru{подруга}\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}friend\textquotedblright{} for a woman. (\textbf{\ru{Подруга}}.) What three pieces build it, and what does each contribute? (\textbf{\ru{По}-} + \textbf{\ru{друг}} + \textbf{-\ru{а}}, the feminine ending.) What English pattern does the same job, on different words? (\textbf{-ess}, as in \emph{host/hostess}.) And what does \emph{\ru{друг}} itself trace back to? (\textbf{PIE \emph{d\textsuperscript{h}rewg\textsuperscript{h}-}, \textquotedblleft{}to accompany, be loyal.\textquotedblright{}})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[brat]{\ru{брат} — \textquotedblleft{}brother,\textquotedblright{} the noun Chapter 5 already warned you about}

\label{lesson:RU-C07-brat}



\begin{quote}
Chapter 5 told you \emph{\ru{брат}} meant \textquotedblleft{}brother\textquotedblright{} and was \textbf{not} related to the verb \emph{\ru{брать}}, \textquotedblleft{}to take\textquotedblright{} — a warning, in passing, about a word not yet properly taught. Here it is, properly taught.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — \ru{брат}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ru{брат}} — \emph{brat} — \textbf{brother}. \textbf{Masculine.}
\end{quote}

Consonant-final, so the ending rule holds a fourth time. And here is the minimal pair Chapter 5 flagged: \textbf{\ru{брат}} (brother) against \textbf{\ru{брать}} (to take, romanized \emph{brat'}) — one soft sign, and nothing else, separates them. Say \emph{brat} with a hard final \emph{t} for \textquotedblleft{}brother\textquotedblright{}; \emph{brat'} with a soft one for \textquotedblleft{}to take.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ru{брат}} is Indo-European *\emph{b\textsuperscript{h}réh\textsubscript{2}tēr} — and this time the resemblance to English is not a trap but the real thing: \textbf{brother} is the same word, inherited, not borrowed. So is Latin \textbf{frāter} ($\to$ \textbf{fraternal}, \textbf{fraternity}), and Sanskrit \textbf{bhrātar}. Few words in any language family are reconstructed with as much confidence as this one.

Recall Chapter 5's other two *\emph{b\textsuperscript{h}}- words, because the three sit right next to each other and mean three different things: \textbf{\ru{брать}} (*\emph{b\textsuperscript{h}er-}, \textquotedblleft{}to carry\textquotedblright{} $\to$ \textbf{bear}, \textbf{birth}), \textbf{\ru{быть}} (*\emph{b\textsuperscript{h}uH-}, \textquotedblleft{}to be\textquotedblright{} $\to$ English \textbf{be}), and now \textbf{\ru{брат}} (*\emph{b\textsuperscript{h}réh\textsubscript{2}tēr}, \textquotedblleft{}brother\textquotedblright{}). Three roots, one shared opening sound, no shared meaning — a family accent, not a family.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\ru{брат}\textquotedblright{} — hard final t, brother
  \item the minimal pair — \textquotedblleft{}\ru{брат}, \ru{брать}\textquotedblright{} — one soft sign apart
  \item \textquotedblleft{}brother, frāter, bhrātar\textquotedblright{} — the same word, three languages
  \item the chapter so far — \textquotedblleft{}\ru{друг}, \ru{подруга}, \ru{брат}\textquotedblright{} (\emph{drug, podrúga, brat})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}brother.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{\ru{Брат}}.) What one sound separates it from \emph{\ru{брать}}, \textquotedblleft{}to take\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{A soft sign} — none in \emph{\ru{брат}}, one in \emph{\ru{брать}}.) Is \emph{\ru{брат}}'s resemblance to English \textbf{brother} real or a trap? (\textbf{Real} — inherited, like Latin \emph{frāter} and Sanskrit \emph{bhrātar}.) Name Chapter 5's two other *\emph{b\textsuperscript{h}}- words, and what each one means. (\textbf{\ru{Быть}}, \textquotedblleft{}to be\textquotedblright{}; \textbf{\ru{брать}}, \textquotedblleft{}to take\textquotedblright{} — three different roots, one shared sound.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sestrá]{\ru{сестра} — \textquotedblleft{}sister,\textquotedblright{} and the chapter closes on four people}

\label{lesson:RU-C07-sestra}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ru{Брат}} (\emph{brat})'s partner, one more secure cognate, and the four people this chapter has introduced you to, gathered in one place.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — \ru{сестра}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ru{сестра}} — \emph{sestrá} — \textbf{sister}. \textbf{Feminine.}
\end{quote}

Ends in \textbf{-\ru{а}}, stress on the end: \emph{ses-TRÁ}. Say \emph{\ru{брат}} and \emph{\ru{сестра}} together and you have both siblings, both genders' endings, in one breath.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ru{сестра}} is Indo-European *\emph{swésōr} — and, like \emph{\ru{брат}}, this is a straight inheritance, not a loan and not a false lead. English \textbf{sister} is the same word (by way of Old Norse, reinforcing an Old English form that had drifted further); Latin's version, \textbf{soror}, took a bumpier sound-change road to the same root. Brother and sister arrive as a matched pair in Russian exactly as they do in the deep history of the whole family.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: who gets \ru{ты}}]
Chapter 2 gave you \textbf{\ru{ты}} for someone close and \textbf{\ru{вы}} for everyone else — the same choice English used to make with \textbf{thou} and \textbf{you}, before \emph{thou} died out and \emph{you} took over both jobs. This chapter has now named exactly who sits on the \emph{\ru{ты}} side of that line: a \textbf{\ru{друг}}, a \textbf{\ru{подруга}}, a \textbf{\ru{брат}}, a \textbf{\ru{сестра}} — the people close enough that formality would be strange. Everyone else still gets \textbf{\ru{вы}}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\ru{сестра}\textquotedblright{} — feminine, stress on the end
  \item the pair — \textquotedblleft{}\ru{брат}, \ru{сестра}\textquotedblright{} — brother, sister
  \item the four people — \textquotedblleft{}\ru{друг}, \ru{подруга}, \ru{брат}, \ru{сестра}\textquotedblright{} (\emph{drug, podrúga, brat, sestrá})
  \item \textquotedblleft{}sister, soror\textquotedblright{} — same root, one smooth, one bumpy
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}sister,\textquotedblright{} with its gender. (\textbf{\ru{Сестра}} — \textbf{feminine}.) Is its resemblance to English \textbf{sister} real? (\textbf{Yes} — both from PIE \emph{*swésōr}.) Name all four people this chapter taught, and which pronoun goes with every one of them. (\textbf{\ru{Друг}, \ru{подруга}, \ru{брат}, \ru{сестра}} — all \textbf{\ru{ты}}.) What pair of English words used to make the same close/distant choice Russian's \ru{ты}/\ru{вы} still makes? (\textbf{Thou} and \textbf{you}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
